feedback: In SDK v2 AutoML, use blocked_models to exclude specific algorithms (e.g., 'TabularDNN') or allowed_models to whitelist only certain ones. This is the equivalent of SDK v1's exclude_list.

question: You have a registered MLflow model in Azure ML. You want to run batch inference on a large CSV file stored in Azure Blob Storage. The results should be written back to Blob Storage. Which Azure ML feature should you use?

options.text: Batch endpoint with a batch deployment
options.explanation: Correct. Batch endpoints in Azure ML are designed for asynchronous, large-scale inference. They read from a data asset or URI, run inference in parallel across a compute cluster, and write results to a specified output location.

options.text: Managed online endpoint with a ManagedOnlineDeployment
options.explanation: Managed online endpoints are for real-time, low-latency inference on single or small batch requests, not for processing large files asynchronously.

options.text: An Azure ML pipeline job with a ParallelRunStep
options.explanation: ParallelRunStep is an SDK v1 concept. While pipelines can do batch scoring, batch endpoints are the SDK v2 native approach for this use case.

options.text: An Azure Databricks job connected to the Azure ML workspace
options.explanation: Databricks can run inference but is not the Azure ML-native solution and adds unnecessary complexity.

feedback: Batch endpoints are the SDK v2 solution for large-scale asynchronous inference. They support MLflow model deployments and can read/write from Azure storage. Invoke with ml_client.batch_endpoints.invoke().

question: You are creating a custom environment for an Azure ML training job. Your team wants to use a curated base image and add the 'lightgbm' and 'shap' Python packages. What is the correct SDK v2 approach?

options.text: Create an Environment object using a conda YAML file or pip requirements and register it with ml_client.environments.create_or_update().
options.explanation: Correct. In SDK v2, you define custom environments with an Environment object specifying a base Docker image and a conda/pip specification file. Register it once and reference it by name:version in job definitions.

options.text: Install packages at job runtime by passing a startup_script to the job configuration.
options.explanation: There is no startup_script parameter in SDK v2 job configuration. Packages should be defined in the environment, not installed at runtime.

options.text: Use a compute cluster with a custom VM image that has the packages pre-installed.
options.explanation: While possible, this is an infrastructure-level solution that is harder to version and maintain compared to Azure ML environments.

options.text: Specify packages directly in the command string using 'pip install lightgbm shap &&' before the training script.
options.explanation: While this works technically, it is not best practice. It adds latency to every run and bypasses the Azure ML environment versioning system.

feedback: Azure ML environments are the standard way to manage Python dependencies. Define using a conda.yaml or requirements.txt, register via ml_client.environments.create_or_update(), then reference by name in CommandJob or component definitions.

question: You need to configure a data monitoring job in Azure ML to detect data drift on a deployed model's input data. What is the correct order of steps using SDK v2?

options.text: Enable data collection on the managed online deployment to capture production input data.
Create a reference dataset (baseline) from the training data as an MLTable data asset.
Define a MonitorSchedule with a DataDriftSignal comparing the production data to the baseline.
Submit the monitor using ml_client.schedules.create_or_update() and review alerts in Azure ML Studio.

feedback: Data drift monitoring requires: (1) a baseline reference dataset from training data, (2) production data collection enabled on the deployment, (3) a MonitorSchedule configured with DataDriftSignal referencing both datasets, and (4) schedule submission. The baseline must exist before the monitor can be defined.

question: You are training a model on an Azure ML compute cluster. The job fails with the error: 'UserError: Resource quota exceeded for Standard_NC6 in region eastus'. What is the most appropriate resolution?

options.text: Request a quota increase for Standard_NC6 in the eastus region through the Azure portal, or switch to a different VM SKU with available quota.
options.explanation: Correct. Azure enforces per-subscription vCPU quotas by VM family and region. When exceeded, you must either request a quota increase via the Azure portal (Subscriptions > Usage + Quotas) or use a different VM family with available quota.

options.text: Increase the max_instances on the compute cluster to allocate more nodes.
options.explanation: Increasing max_instances will not help if the underlying VM quota is already exceeded. The cluster cannot provision nodes beyond the quota limit.

options.text: Restart the compute cluster to reset the quota counter.
options.explanation: Azure subscription quotas are not reset by restarting resources. Quota is a hard subscription-level limit.

options.text: Move the workspace to a different resource group to get a fresh quota allocation.
options.explanation: Quotas are per subscription and region, not per resource group. Moving the workspace does not affect quota.

feedback: VM quota errors require either a quota increase request via the Azure portal or using a different VM SKU. Quota is enforced at the subscription and region level, per VM family.

question: You are configuring an Azure ML compute cluster for training jobs. Which of the following properties are valid configuration options for an AmlCompute cluster? Select all that apply.
feedback: Valid AmlCompute properties include min_instances, max_instances, vm_priority (dedicated vs spot/low_priority), and idle_time_before_scale_down. There is no 'auto_scale_threshold' or 'enable_gpu_monitoring' property in the AmlCompute configuration.

question: In Azure ML SDK v2, you can use a serverless compute target (no pre-created cluster required) to run command jobs by simply specifying the VM size in the job configuration.

options.explanation: Correct. Azure ML SDK v2 supports serverless compute, where you specify the VM size directly in the job (e.g., resources=ResourceConfiguration(instance_type='Standard_DS3_v2')) without needing a named compute cluster.
Serverless compute is a supported feature in SDK v2. It removes the need to pre-create and manage compute clusters for individual jobs.

feedback: SDK v2 introduced serverless compute support. You can specify compute inline in a job without pre-creating a named cluster, using the instance_type parameter in ResourceConfiguration.

question: You are using Azure ML's Responsible AI dashboard to evaluate a classification model. You want to identify which features most strongly influenced a specific incorrect prediction. Which Responsible AI component provides this capability?

options.explanation: Correct. The Model Explainability component in the Responsible AI dashboard uses SHAP values to show per-instance (local) feature importance, revealing which features drove a specific prediction.
Error Analysis identifies cohorts or subgroups where the model performs poorly, but does not explain individual feature contributions for a specific prediction.
The Data Analysis component shows dataset statistics and distributions, not individual prediction explanations.
Fairness Assessment evaluates model performance across demographic groups, not individual prediction explanations.

feedback: The Responsible AI dashboard's Model Explainability component provides both global feature importance (across all predictions) and local feature importance (for individual predictions) using SHAP. Use local explanations to debug specific incorrect predictions.

question: You need to share a registered data asset in Azure ML with a colleague in the same workspace so they can use it in their training jobs. Which of the following statements are true about Azure ML data assets? Select all that apply.

options.text: Data assets registered in a workspace are accessible to all users with appropriate RBAC permissions in that workspace.
options.explanation: Correct. Registered data assets are workspace-level resources. Any user with at least Reader or Contributor RBAC role can access and use them in jobs.

options.text: A data asset can point to data in Azure Blob Storage, Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2, or a local path.
options.explanation: Correct. Azure ML data assets support references to Azure Blob, ADLS Gen2, and local paths (which get uploaded to the default workspace datastore).

options.text: Registering a data asset copies all the data into the Azure ML workspace storage.
options.explanation: Incorrect. Data assets are references (pointers) to data locations. Registering an asset does not copy the data; it stores the URI and metadata.

options.text: Data assets are versioned, allowing you to track which version of data was used for a specific training job.
options.explanation: Correct. Azure ML data assets support versioning. Each run logs which data asset version was used, enabling reproducibility.

feedback: Data assets in Azure ML are versioned, workspace-scoped references to data (not copies). They support Blob, ADLS Gen2, and local paths, and are accessible to all authorized workspace users.

question: You run a hyperparameter sweep job in Azure ML SDK v2. You want to maximize 'val_f1_score' and stop trials early if they are unlikely to outperform the best run so far. Which early termination policy should you use?

options.explanation: Correct. BanditPolicy terminates trials where the primary metric falls outside a specified slack factor/amount relative to the best performing run. It is ideal for maximizing a metric by cutting unpromising trials early.

MedianStoppingPolicy cancels runs whose primary metric is worse than the median of completed runs at that interval. It is less aggressive than BanditPolicy and less precise for maximizing a specific metric.
TruncationSelectionPolicy cancels a percentage of the lowest-performing runs at each evaluation interval. It works differently from BanditPolicy and is less commonly used.
NoTerminationPolicy runs all trials to completion with no early stopping, which is the opposite of what is needed here.

feedback: BanditPolicy is the most common early termination policy for sweep jobs. It stops trials that fall outside a slack_factor relative to the best run, saving compute costs during hyperparameter tuning.

question:
You are a data scientist at a healthcare company. You have trained an XGBoost model locally and registered it in Azure Machine Learning. You need to deploy it as a real-time endpoint that can handle bursts of up to 500 requests per second, requires sub-100ms latency, and must scale to zero when idle to minimize cost.

Which deployment configuration should you use?

options.text: Azure Container Instance (ACI) with a single-instance managed online endpoint
Managed online endpoint with deployment autoscaling configured via az ml online-deployment update, setting min_instances=0 and scale_type=TargetUtilizationScaling
Batch endpoint with a compute cluster of min_instances=0 and max_instances=10
Kubernetes online endpoint on AKS with manual scaling rules defined in the deployment YAML

feedback: Managed online endpoints support autoscaling to zero with TargetUtilizationScaling, meeting latency and scale-to-zero requirements. ACI doesn't autoscale. Batch endpoints are not for real-time sub-100ms latency. AKS requires manual scaling management and doesn't scale to zero natively without additional configuration.

question:
You have a training pipeline built with Azure ML SDK v2. The pipeline reads a registered data asset, trains a model, and registers the output. During a pipeline run, you receive this error:

    UserError: The data asset version 'training_data:3' could not be resolved.

You need to fix the pipeline so it always uses the latest version of the data asset without hardcoding version numbers.

Which TWO changes should you make?

options.text: Replace the versioned reference with ml_client.data.get('training_data', label='latest') to resolve the latest version at submission time
Set the data asset version to 'latest' as a string literal in the Input() definition
Use azureml://datastores/... URI with @latest label in the Input path parameter
Register a new fixed version of the data asset before each pipeline run using ml_client.data.create_or_update()

feedback: Both ml_client.data.get() with label='latest' and the @latest URI label are the correct SDK v2 patterns for resolving the latest data asset version dynamically. 'latest' as a string literal is not a valid version value. Registering a new version each run adds unnecessary overhead and doesn't solve the dynamic resolution problem.

question:
Your team is building a computer vision pipeline that fine-tunes a PyTorch model on a GPU cluster. The job runs successfully on a single node but fails with a NCCL error when scaled to 4 nodes:

    NCCL error: unhandled system error / ncclSystemError

The compute cluster uses Standard_NC6s_v3 VMs. Networking is configured with the default VNet.

What is the MOST LIKELY cause and fix?

options.text: The model is too large for multi-node training; switch to Standard_ND40rs_v2 VMs with InfiniBand support

NCCL requires InfiniBand or RDMA-enabled VMs for multi-node GPU communication; Standard_NC6s_v3 does not support InfiniBand. Switch to an ND-series VM that supports InfiniBand and ensure the VNet allows RDMA traffic.
Increase the process_count_per_node to match the number of GPUs per VM and set node_count=1
Switch the distribution strategy from PyTorch to MPI to avoid NCCL dependency

feedback: NCCL multi-node errors on Azure are almost always caused by using VM SKUs that lack InfiniBand/RDMA support. NC-series VMs use standard Ethernet for inter-node communication, which causes NCCL system errors at scale. ND-series (e.g. ND40rs_v2) supports InfiniBand. Switching distribution type doesn't fix the underlying network hardware limitation.

question:
You are operationalizing an ML model using Azure ML pipelines. The pipeline has three sequential components: data_prep, train, and evaluate. The evaluate component outputs a metric called 'val_accuracy'. You want the pipeline to automatically register the model ONLY if val_accuracy >= 0.85, without manual intervention.

How should you implement this?

options.text: Add an if/else block in the pipeline YAML to conditionally run the register_model component based on the evaluate output
Use a Control Flow component (condition node) in the pipeline that reads the val_accuracy output and only executes the register_model step if the threshold is met
Within the evaluate component script, check val_accuracy and call ml_client.models.create_or_update() conditionally inside the component code before the component exits
Configure a Pipeline Schedule with a metric-based trigger on val_accuracy >= 0.85 in the Azure ML studio UI

feedback: Azure ML SDK v2 pipelines do not natively support conditional branching between components at the pipeline graph level (no if/else in YAML or condition nodes as of current SDK v2). The correct pattern is to embed the conditional registration logic inside the evaluate component itself using ml_client within the component script. Pipeline schedules are time-based, not metric-based.

question:
You built a churn prediction model and deployed it to a managed online endpoint. Three weeks after deployment, you notice prediction quality has degraded. You want to set up monitoring so you are automatically alerted when data drift exceeds a threshold in the future.

Which TWO actions are required to enable this?

options.text: Enable data collection on the online deployment by setting data_collector in the deployment definition to capture inputs and outputs
Create a model monitor using ml_client.model_monitors.create_or_update() with a reference dataset and drift threshold alerts configured
Configure Application Insights in the Azure ML workspace to track feature distributions automatically
Register a new version of the model with monitoring=True to activate drift detection

feedback: Data drift monitoring in Azure ML requires two things: (1) data collection enabled on the deployment so production inputs/outputs are captured, and (2) a Model Monitor configured with a reference dataset and alert thresholds. Application Insights tracks telemetry/latency, not feature drift. There is no monitoring=True flag on model registration.

question:
You are running an AutoML classification job on a tabular dataset with 2 million rows. The job is taking over 6 hours and you need it to complete within 2 hours. Your dataset has 40 features, some of which are high-cardinality categoricals.

Which combination of AutoML settings will MOST effectively reduce run time while preserving model quality?

options.text: Set enable_early_termination=True, experiment_timeout_hours=2, and max_concurrent_iterations=8 on a cluster with 8 nodes
Set experiment_timeout_hours=2, max_concurrent_iterations=8, featurization='auto', and enable_stack_ensemble=False on a cluster with 8 nodes
Enable enable_onnx_compatible_models=True and set featurization='off' to reduce preprocessing overhead

feedback: The most impactful levers are: (1) parallelism via max_concurrent_iterations matching node count, (2) disabling stack ensemble which adds significant time at the end with marginal gain, and (3) letting featurization='auto' handle categoricals correctly. Blocking strong models like XGBoost/LightGBM hurts quality. ONNX compatibility and featurization='off' don't address speed meaningfully and the latter degrades quality on high-cardinality features.

question:
You need to train a model that requires a custom Docker image with a proprietary C++ library that cannot be installed via pip. The training job must run on Azure ML compute clusters and the image must be rebuilt only when the Dockerfile changes, not on every job submission.

What is the correct approach?

options.text: Use a custom Environment with build.dockerfile_path pointing to your Dockerfile; Azure ML will build and cache the image in the workspace's Azure Container Registry on first use and reuse it on subsequent runs
Package the C++ library as a pip wheel and install it via conda_file in the Environment definition
Upload the Dockerfile to a datastore and reference it as a data input in the training job YAML
Use a base curated environment and add a setup_script parameter to install the library at job start time on every run

feedback: Azure ML Environments built from a Dockerfile are built once and cached in ACR. On subsequent job submissions with the same Environment version, the cached image is reused â€” no rebuild occurs unless you create a new Environment version. Pip wheels require the library to be pip-installable. Datastores are for data, not build contexts. setup_script runs on every job start, not just when the image changes.

question:
You have an ML pipeline that retrains a model weekly. After last week's run, a downstream team reports that the registered model is producing different predictions than expected. You need to investigate what changed.

Which TWO Azure ML features should you use to diagnose the issue?

options.text: Open the pipeline run in Azure ML Studio and inspect the lineage view to trace which dataset version and code snapshot were used in the run that produced the registered model
Use mlflow.get_run() to retrieve logged metrics and parameters from the run associated with the registered model version
Re-run the pipeline with the same compute cluster to reproduce the issue deterministically
Compare the model's conda environment YAML files between the current and previous registered versions in the Models registry

feedback: The lineage view in Azure ML Studio shows exactly which data asset version, code snapshot, and environment were used â€” this is the first thing to check when a model changes unexpectedly. mlflow.get_run() lets you pull the exact hyperparameters and metrics logged. Re-running doesn't diagnose root cause. Comparing conda YAMLs only catches dependency changes, not data or hyperparameter drift.

question:
You are designing a responsible AI evaluation for a binary classification model used in loan approvals. The model shows 91% overall accuracy, but your Responsible AI dashboard reveals that the false negative rate is 34% for applicants aged 18-25 compared to 8% for applicants aged 40-60.

What does this indicate, and what is the appropriate next step?

options.text: The model has high overall accuracy so the disparity is within acceptable range; proceed to deployment

The model exhibits disparate impact on younger applicants; use the Error Analysis component in the Responsible AI dashboard to identify which features drive the disparity, then apply fairness-aware reweighting or threshold adjustment per cohort
Retrain the model with age removed as a feature to eliminate the bias
Switch to a more complex model (e.g. deep neural network) to improve overall accuracy and reduce the per-cohort disparity

feedback: A 34% vs 8% false negative rate across age groups is a significant fairness violation (disparate impact) regardless of overall accuracy. The RAI dashboard's Error Analysis component identifies root-cause features driving cohort disparities. Removing age doesn't fix proxy features. More complex models often amplify bias. Threshold adjustment per cohort is a valid fairness intervention supported by Azure ML's RAI toolbox.

question:
You need to run hyperparameter tuning for a deep learning model. The search space has 3 continuous parameters and 1 discrete parameter with 5 values. You want to find a good configuration within 20 total runs and terminate poorly-performing runs early.

Which sweep job configuration is MOST appropriate?

options.text: sampling_algorithm: bayesian, max_total_trials: 20, early_termination: BanditPolicy(slack_factor=0.15, evaluation_interval=5)

feedback: Bayesian sampling is optimal for mixed continuous/discrete spaces with a limited budget (20 runs) because it uses prior results to guide exploration intelligently. BanditPolicy terminates runs whose primary metric falls outside a slack margin of the best run, which works well with Bayesian sampling's sequential nature. Grid search is only practical for purely discrete spaces. MedianStoppingPolicy requires more runs to be statistically meaningful. TruncationSelectionPolicy is less compatible with Bayesian sampling's sequential dependency.

question:
You need to develop a solution using Azure OpenAI Service that supports advanced reasoning and problem-solving tasks such as complex math and science questions.

Which model should you use?
feedback: The o1 model (and o-series models like DeepSeek-R1) are specifically designed for advanced reasoning, math, and science tasks. gpt-35-turbo is a general chat model, whisper is for speech-to-text, and dall-e-3 generates images.

question:
Your organization needs to translate documents into Arabic with high cultural and linguistic accuracy. You are selecting a model from the Azure AI Foundry model catalog.

Which model is the BEST choice?
feedback: Core42 JAIS is an Arabic-focused LLM optimized for Arabic language tasks and cultural context. Mistral Large focuses on European languages. Llama 3 and Phi-3 are general-purpose models without Arabic specialization.

question:
You are selecting a language model from the Azure AI Foundry catalog for a use case that requires analyzing both images and text in the same request.

Which TWO models support multimodal (image + text) input?
feedback: GPT-4o and Phi-3-vision are both multimodal models capable of analyzing images and text together. gpt-35-turbo is text-only. Whisper is a speech-to-text model, not a multimodal vision model.

question:
You are building a generative AI application using the Azure AI Foundry SDK. You need to connect your Python app to an Azure AI Foundry project.

Which object should you instantiate first?
feedback: AIProjectClient is the main entry point for the Azure AI Foundry SDK. It is created using a project connection string and DefaultAzureCredential, and provides access to inference, connections, and other project resources. Other clients are created from it, not independently.

question:
You are developing a chat application using Azure AI Foundry SDK. You want to switch between different deployed models (e.g. from phi-4 to gpt-4) without changing your authentication or connection logic.

Which deployment type should you use?

options.text: Serverless API â€” each model gets its own unique endpoint
Managed Compute â€” models deployed to custom compute with individual endpoints
Azure AI Model Inference â€” unified endpoint supporting multiple model types via an Azure AI services resource
Azure OpenAI Service â€” dedicated endpoint for OpenAI models only

feedback: Azure AI Model Inference provides a unified endpoint that supports OpenAI and other catalog models. You can switch models by just changing the model name in your code. Serverless API and Managed Compute give each model its own endpoint. Azure OpenAI Service only supports OpenAI models.

question: You are optimizing a generative AI model before deploying it to production. Arrange the following optimization steps in the correct order as recommended by Azure AI Foundry best practices.

options.text: Apply prompt engineering with clear instructions and structured format
Update system messages with specific use case examples and chain-of-thought context
Apply model tuning via fine-tuning or RAG with a specific data source
Deploy the optimized model to a production endpoint

feedback: Azure AI Foundry recommends this sequence before deployment: (1) Prompt engineering first as it costs nothing, (2) System message refinement with examples and chain-of-thought, (3) Model tuning via fine-tuning or RAG if prompting alone is insufficient, (4) Deploy to endpoint. Each step builds on the last.

question:
You are building a RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) solution using Azure AI Foundry. You have uploaded documents to Azure Blob Storage. You need to make the documents searchable so the AI model can retrieve relevant context based on user queries â€” including queries that use different words than those in the documents.

Which Azure service and search method should you use?

options.text: Azure AI Search with keyword search only
Azure Blob Storage with semantic search enabled directly on the container
Azure AI Search with vector search using embeddings to enable semantic similarity matching
Azure AI Language with named entity recognition to index document content

feedback: Azure AI Search with vector search (embeddings) enables retrieval based on semantic similarity â€” meaning queries using different words than the documents can still match relevant content by comparing vector distances (cosine similarity). Keyword search only matches exact terms. Blob Storage has no built-in semantic search. Azure AI Language does NLP tasks but is not a retrieval/indexing service.

question:
You are evaluating a prompt flow application in Azure AI Foundry. You need to track metrics that measure the quality of generated responses.

Which THREE metrics are standard evaluation metrics for LLM-based applications in Azure AI Foundry?

options.text: Groundedness â€” alignment between model output and the source data
Fluency â€” grammatical correctness and natural language quality of responses
Coherence â€” logical flow and readability of the output
Utilization â€” percentage of retrieved chunks used in the response

feedback: Groundedness, Fluency, and Coherence are three of the five standard Azure AI Foundry evaluation metrics (along with Relevance and Similarity). Utilization is related to RAG retrieval analysis but is not one of the five standard prompt flow evaluation metrics.

question:
You are building a RAG solution. During evaluation, the system shows HIGH groundedness but LOW relevance scores.

What does this combination indicate?

options.text: The model is hallucinating â€” answers are not based on the retrieved documents
The model answers are factually grounded in the documents, but the retrieved documents are not relevant to the user's actual question
The retrieval system is returning too many chunks, causing the model to be confused
The model output is grammatically poor and hard to read

feedback: High groundedness means the model's answers are well-anchored to the retrieved content (not hallucinating). Low relevance means the retrieved content itself wasn't pertinent to the user's query â€” a retrieval quality problem, not a generation problem. The fix is improving the retrieval/indexing step, not the model.

question:
You are evaluating two RAG solutions. Solution A shows low completeness and high groundedness. Solution B shows high completeness but low groundedness.

Which statement correctly describes the issue with each solution?

options.text: Solution A is hallucinating; Solution B is missing information from its answers
Solution A's answers are factually anchored but incomplete; Solution B's answers are comprehensive but not grounded in the source data
Solution A has poor retrieval; Solution B has poor generation quality
Both solutions have the same underlying problem â€” poor chunk size configuration

feedback: Completeness measures whether the answer covers all relevant information. Groundedness measures whether the answer is based on retrieved source data. Low completeness + high groundedness = answers are accurate but missing content (fix: increase chunk size or top-k). High completeness + low groundedness = answers cover the topic but are hallucinated/not anchored in sources (fix: improve retrieval relevance and grounding).

question:
A RAG solution evaluation shows low completeness scores. A data scientist recommends increasing the chunk size.

Why would increasing chunk size improve completeness?

options.text: Larger chunks reduce the number of API calls needed during retrieval
Larger chunks provide more context per retrieved piece, reducing information loss at chunk boundaries so the model has more complete content to generate answers from
Larger chunks improve vector embedding quality by including more tokens
Larger chunks lower the top-k parameter needed, reducing retrieval cost

feedback: When chunks are too small, relevant information gets split across chunk boundaries and some of it may not be retrieved. Increasing chunk size keeps more related content together in a single retrieved piece, giving the model a more complete picture to generate a full answer from. This directly addresses low completeness.

question:
You need to fine-tune a GPT model in Azure AI Foundry for a customer support use case. You want the model to learn to answer only Xbox-related questions and decline off-topic requests.

What format must your training data be in?

options.text: CSV file with columns: system_prompt, user_input, assistant_output
JSON file with a flat list of question-answer pairs
JSONL file where each line is a full chat interaction with system, user, and assistant messages
Parquet file with tokenized input-output pairs

feedback: Azure AI Foundry fine-tuning requires JSONL (JSON Lines) format where each line represents a complete chat interaction containing role-based messages: system (persona/instructions), user (input), and assistant (expected output). This mirrors the chat completions format the model was originally trained on.

question:
You are fine-tuning a model in Azure AI Foundry and want the model to learn from specific assistant responses while ignoring others. For example, you want to exclude a short intermediate response ('Paris') and only train on the more elaborated sarcastic response.

How do you configure this in your JSONL training data?

options.text: Remove the excluded message entries entirely from the JSONL file
Set weight: 0 on messages to exclude from training and weight: 1 on messages to include
Add a trainable: false flag to the message role field
Place excluded messages in a separate validation JSONL file

feedback: Azure AI Foundry fine-tuning supports a weight key on assistant messages. weight: 0 tells the trainer to ignore that message during loss calculation (not learned from), while weight: 1 includes it. This lets you keep conversation context intact while selectively controlling which responses the model trains on.

question: You are configuring a fine-tuning job in Azure AI Foundry and need to control training behavior. Which TWO parameters directly influence how the model learns during fine-tuning?

options.text: n_epochs â€” controls how many times the model trains over the full dataset
learning_rate_multiplier â€” scales the base learning rate during training
chunk_size â€” determines how training documents are split for indexing
top_k â€” controls how many results are retrieved during evaluation

feedback: n_epochs and learning_rate_multiplier are both standard fine-tuning hyperparameters supported in Azure AI Foundry. chunk_size is a RAG/indexing parameter, not a fine-tuning parameter. top_k is a retrieval parameter used in RAG, not fine-tuning.

question:
You are building a Prompt Flow in Azure AI Foundry. You want to test two different system message styles to see which produces more accurate responses.

Which Prompt Flow feature supports this?

options.text: Flow types â€” switch between Standard, Chat, and Evaluation flows
Runtimes â€” configure different compute environments per flow run
Variants â€” create multiple versions of an LLM node with different configurations to compare outputs
Connections â€” link to different Azure OpenAI resources for each test

feedback: Variants in Prompt Flow allow you to create multiple versions of an LLM node with different prompts, system messages, or parameters. Currently variants are only supported on LLM nodes. This lets you A/B test prompt configurations efficiently without duplicating the entire flow.

question:
You are designing an Azure AI Foundry hub for a team of 10 data scientists working on 3 separate AI projects. Each project should share access to the same Azure AI services connection and storage, but manage their own models and experiments independently.

What is the correct resource structure?

options.text: Create 3 separate hubs, one per project, each with their own shared resources
Create 1 hub with shared resources and connections, then create 3 projects within the hub â€” one per team
Create 1 project and use role-based access control to partition work between teams
Create 1 hub and 1 project, and use compute instances to isolate each team's work

feedback: A Hub is a shared container for resources, connections, and security config across multiple projects. Projects within a hub share the hub's resources but manage their own assets independently. This is exactly the designed pattern â€” one hub, multiple projects per team. You need at least one hub to use AI Foundry's full solution development features.

question:
A team member needs full access to an Azure AI Foundry hub â€” including the ability to create new hubs and manage permissions on existing resources.

Which role should they be assigned?
feedback: Owner has full access including creating new hubs and managing hub permissions. Contributor has the same access as Owner but cannot manage hub permissions. Azure AI Developer cannot create hubs or manage permissions. Azure AI Inference Deployment Operator only has permissions to create resource deployments within a resource group.

question:
You need to select a model benchmark metric that measures whether a model's output is factually aligned with the input data provided â€” for example, in a RAG scenario where you want to verify the model is not hallucinating.

Which benchmark metric should you use?
feedback: Groundedness specifically measures alignment between the model's generated answers and the input/source data â€” making it the correct metric for detecting hallucination in RAG scenarios. Fluency measures grammatical quality. Coherence measures logical flow. GPT Similarity measures semantic similarity to a ground truth answer, not alignment with source data.

question:
You are building a Prompt Flow in Azure AI Foundry that needs to connect securely to an Azure OpenAI resource. You want to store the API credentials safely so they are not hardcoded in your flow.

Where does Prompt Flow store connection credentials?

options.text: In the prompt flow YAML configuration file in the project repository
In an environment variable on the compute instance runtime
In Azure Key Vault, managed through the Prompt Flow connections configuration
In the Azure AI Foundry project settings as plain text connection strings

feedback: Prompt Flow connections store credentials (API keys, endpoints) securely in Azure Key Vault. This keeps sensitive information out of code and configuration files. The connections UI in Azure AI Foundry is the interface for managing these, but the underlying storage is Key Vault.

question:
You are using the Azure AI Foundry SDK to build a Python app that uses Azure AI Language service for sentiment analysis. You want to retrieve the default Azure AI services connection from your project, including its API key.

Which method call correctly retrieves this connection with credentials?
feedback: connections.get_default() retrieves the default connection of a specified type. Setting include_credentials=True returns the API key needed to authenticate downstream clients like TextAnalyticsClient. connections.list() returns all connections without filtering to default. connections.get() requires a specific connection name. get_chat_completions_client() is for inference, not connection retrieval.

question: You are creating a command job in Azure ML SDK v2. What is the correct import to use the command() function?
code_html: from azure.ai.ml import ???, Input job = ???( code="./src", command="python train.py", environment="AzureML-sklearn-0.24@latest", compute="aml-cluster" )
feedback: The correct import and function is 'command' from azure.ai.ml. It is used to configure and submit a single script as a command job. 'pipeline' is for multi-step workflows, 'sweep' is for hyperparameter tuning.

question: You need to track all metrics automatically for a scikit-learn model in an Azure ML job. Which function call enables automatic MLflow logging?
code_html: import mlflow # Enable automatic logging of all metrics, # parameters, and artifacts mlflow.???()
feedback: mlflow.autolog() enables automatic logging for supported libraries (sklearn, XGBoost, etc.) including parameters, metrics, and model artifacts. start_run() opens a run context manually. log_metric() logs a single metric. set_tracking_uri() points MLflow to a tracking server.

question: You are logging model evaluation metrics in an Azure ML training script. Which MLflow function should you use to log a single numeric metric like accuracy?
code_html: import mlflow acc = 0.94 auc = 0.97 # Log accuracy as a tracked metric mlflow.???("Accuracy", acc) mlflow.???("AUC", auc)
feedback: mlflow.log_metric() logs a single key-value numeric metric (like accuracy, AUC). log_param() is for hyperparameters/settings. log_artifact() is for files like plots or model binaries. log_model() registers a model object.

question: You want to save a ROC curve plot as a tracked artifact in your Azure ML job using MLflow. Which function should you use?
code_html: import mlflow import matplotlib.pyplot as plt plt.savefig("ROC-Curve.png") # Save the plot as a tracked artifact mlflow.???("ROC-Curve.png")
feedback: mlflow.log_artifact() logs a file (like a PNG plot) as a tracked artifact, visible in the Output+logs tab of the Azure ML job. log_metric() is for numbers only. log_param() is for key-value parameters. log_image() is not a standard MLflow function.

question: You are configuring an AutoML classification job in Azure ML SDK v2. Which parameter specifies the column the model should predict?
code_html: from azure.ai.ml import automl classification_job = automl.classification( compute="aml-cluster", experiment_name="auto-ml-class", training_data=my_training_data_input, ???="Diabetic", primary_metric="accuracy", n_cross_validations=5 )
feedback: In Azure ML SDK v2, AutoML uses target_column_name to specify the column to predict. This is different from older SDK v1 syntax. label_column, output_column, and y_column are not valid parameter names in this context.

question: You need to prevent AutoML from using LogisticRegression during training. Which parameter and method should you use?
code_html: # Block specific algorithms from AutoML classification_job.???( ???=["LogisticRegression"], enable_onnx_compatible_models=True )
feedback: The correct method is set_training() with the blocked_training_algorithms parameter. set_limits() controls timeouts and trial counts, not algorithm selection. excluded_models and skip_algorithms are not valid parameter names.

question: You are configuring an AutoML job and need to limit it to run for no more than 60 minutes total, with each trial capped at 20 minutes. Which method and parameters should you use?
code_html: classification_job.???( ???=60, trial_timeout_minutes=20, max_trials=5, enable_early_termination=True )
feedback: set_limits() is the correct method for controlling compute constraints. timeout_minutes sets the total AutoML experiment time. set_training() handles algorithm configuration, not time limits. experiment_timeout is not a valid parameter name in SDK v2.

question: You are creating a sweep job for hyperparameter tuning. You want to maximize accuracy using grid sampling across 3 regularization values. What goes in the blank?
code_html: from azure.ai.ml.sweep import Choice command_job_for_sweep = job( reg_rate=Choice(values=[0.01, 0.1, 1]) ) sweep_job = command_job_for_sweep.sweep( compute="aml-cluster", sampling_algorithm="???", primary_metric="training_accuracy_score", goal="???" )
feedback: Grid sampling tries every combination â€” correct when you have discrete values like Choice([0.01, 0.1, 1]). The goal parameter must be 'Maximize' (capital M) or 'Minimize' â€” these are the only valid values. 'max' is not valid.

question: You are defining a managed online endpoint in Azure ML. The endpoint name must be unique. Which class and auth_mode value should you use for key-based authentication?
code_html: from azure.ai.ml.entities import ??? endpoint = ???( name=online_endpoint_name, description="My endpoint", auth_mode="???" ) ml_client.begin_create_or_update(endpoint).result()
feedback: ManagedOnlineEndpoint is the correct class for creating an online endpoint. auth_mode="key" enables key-based authentication. ManagedOnlineDeployment is for configuring what runs behind the endpoint (the model/container), not the endpoint itself. "token" uses AAD tokens, not keys.

question: You are writing a scoring script for a custom model deployment. Which two functions are required in every scoring script?
code_html: import json, joblib, numpy as np, os def ???(): global model model_path = os.path.join( os.getenv('AZUREML_MODEL_DIR'), 'model.pkl' ) model = joblib.load(model_path) def ???(raw_data): data = np.array(json.loads(raw_data)['data']) predictions = model.predict(data) return predictions.tolist()
feedback: Every Azure ML scoring script requires exactly two functions: init() to load the model into memory when the container starts, and run(data) to process each inference request. These function names are mandatory â€” Azure ML calls them by name.

question: You have deployed a blue deployment to an online endpoint and want to send 100% of traffic to it. Which code correctly assigns all traffic to the blue deployment?
feedback: The correct attribute is endpoint.traffic and the value is an integer 100 (representing 100%). The dictionary maps deployment name to percentage. 1.0 and 1 are not valid â€” traffic values must sum to 100 as integers.

question: You are configuring a managed online deployment using an MLflow model. Which AssetType value correctly identifies it as an MLflow model?
code_html: from azure.ai.ml.entities import Model, ManagedOnlineDeployment from azure.ai.ml.constants import AssetTypes model = Model( path="./model", type=AssetTypes.???, description="my mlflow model" )
feedback: AssetTypes.MLFLOW_MODEL tells Azure ML the model is in MLflow format, which allows it to use the built-in MLflow inference server (no scoring script needed). URI_FILE is for a single file reference. MLTABLE is for tabular data. CUSTOM_MODEL requires a scoring script.

question: You need to create an MLClient to connect to your Azure ML workspace. Which credential class should you try first, falling back to InteractiveBrowserCredential only on failure?
code_html: from azure.identity import ???, InteractiveBrowserCredential from azure.ai.ml import MLClient try: credential = ???() credential.get_token("https://management.azure.com/.default") except Exception as ex: credential = InteractiveBrowserCredential() ml_client = MLClient.from_config(credential=credential)
feedback: DefaultAzureCredential is the recommended first choice â€” it tries multiple auth methods automatically (env vars, managed identity, Azure CLI, VS Code, etc.). If it fails, fall back to InteractiveBrowserCredential for interactive login. The others require explicit configuration.

question: You are configuring a training input using an MLTable data asset registered in Azure ML. Which AssetType and path format should you use?
code_html: from azure.ai.ml.constants import AssetTypes from azure.ai.ml import Input my_training_data_input = Input( type=AssetTypes.???, path="azureml:diabetes-training:???" )
feedback: AutoML requires MLTable format (AssetTypes.MLTABLE), not URI_FILE or URI_FOLDER. The path uses the azureml: protocol with the registered data asset name and a specific integer version number. 'latest' as a string literal is not valid here â€” use a version number.

question: You need to invoke a deployed online endpoint to get predictions. Which method and parameter correctly calls the endpoint with a JSON test file?
code_html: response = ml_client.online_endpoints.???( endpoint_name=online_endpoint_name, deployment_name="blue", ???="sample-data.json" ) print(response)
feedback: ml_client.online_endpoints.invoke() is the correct method to call an online endpoint. The parameter to pass a JSON file is request_file. predict() and score() are not methods on the online_endpoints client. input_file and input_data are not valid parameter names.

question:
You configure a sweep job with the following early termination policy:

    slack_amount = 0.2
    delay_evaluation = 5
    evaluation_interval = 1

What does this configuration do?

options.text: Terminate any trial whose metric falls more than 0.2 below the best trial so far, evaluated every trial starting from trial 6
Terminate any trial whose metric falls more than 20% below the average, starting from the first trial
Stop the entire sweep job after 5 trials if accuracy does not improve by 0.2
Terminate any trial that runs longer than 0.2 minutes, checked every 5 trials

feedback: This is a Bandit Policy. slack_amount=0.2 means any trial whose primary metric is more than 0.2 behind the best trial is terminated. delay_evaluation=5 means the policy doesn't start until after trial 5. evaluation_interval=1 means it checks every trial after that. Slack is an absolute margin, not a percentage.

question:
You are running a sweep job and want to terminate poorly performing trials automatically. A trial should be stopped if its primary metric is more than 0.2 units behind the best trial seen so far, but only after the first 10 trials have completed.

Which policy and configuration should you use?
feedback: BanditPolicy with slack_amount terminates trials that fall more than a fixed amount behind the best metric. delay_evaluation=10 means it won't start until 10 trials are done. MedianStoppingPolicy uses the median of running averages, not a fixed slack margin. TruncationSelectionPolicy terminates the bottom X% â€” not a fixed margin from the best.

question: What is the difference between slack_amount and slack_factor in a Bandit Policy?

options.text: slack_amount is a fixed absolute margin; slack_factor is a ratio relative to the best metric value
slack_amount is a percentage; slack_factor is an absolute value
They are interchangeable â€” both define a percentage threshold
slack_factor applies to discrete hyperparameters; slack_amount applies to continuous

feedback: slack_amount sets an absolute gap â€” e.g. if best metric is 0.9 and slack_amount=0.2, anything below 0.7 is terminated. slack_factor sets a relative ratio â€” e.g. slack_factor=0.1 means anything more than 10% behind the best metric is terminated. You use one or the other, not both.

question:
You configure a sweep job with MedianStoppingPolicy(evaluation_interval=5, delay_evaluation=10).

What happens to a trial under this policy?

options.text: A trial is stopped if its metric at any evaluation point falls below the median of all completed trials' metrics, checked every 5 trials after the first 10
A trial is stopped if it runs longer than the median trial duration, starting from trial 10
A trial is stopped if it is in the bottom 50% of all trials, checked once at trial 5
A trial is stopped if its metric is more than 5 units below the median, after 10 evaluations

feedback: MedianStoppingPolicy computes the running average of primary metrics across all trials and terminates any trial whose reported metric falls below the median of those running averages. evaluation_interval=5 means it checks every 5 intervals, delay_evaluation=10 means it won't start until interval 10.

question:
You configure a TruncationSelectionPolicy(truncation_percentage=20, evaluation_interval=1, delay_evaluation=5).

What does this policy do?

options.text: Terminates the bottom 20% of trials at each evaluation interval, starting after 5 trials
Terminates any trial that is more than 20% below the best trial, starting after 5 trials
Stops the sweep if fewer than 20% of trials improve, after 5 evaluations
Selects the top 20% of trials and stops all others immediately

feedback: TruncationSelectionPolicy cancels the bottom X% of trials at each evaluation point. With truncation_percentage=20, the worst-performing 20% are terminated at each check. This is different from BanditPolicy (which uses a margin from the best) and MedianStoppingPolicy (which uses the median).

question:
You are running a sweep job and want to stop trials that are clearly underperforming compared to the best trial, as early as possible. Compute budget is limited. You have continuous hyperparameters.

Which early termination policy is MOST appropriate?

options.text: No early termination policy â€” let all trials complete
MedianStoppingPolicy â€” terminates trials below the running median
BanditPolicy â€” terminates trials that fall outside a slack margin from the best trial
TruncationSelectionPolicy â€” terminates the bottom percentage of trials

feedback: BanditPolicy is best for aggressive early termination against the best-performing trial, which is ideal for limited compute with continuous hyperparameters. It terminates a trial as soon as it falls outside the slack margin of the current best â€” more aggressive than Median or Truncation. No policy wastes compute.

question: What does the evaluation_interval parameter control in an early termination policy?

options.text: The number of trials to skip before the policy activates
How frequently (in intervals/steps) the policy is applied to evaluate whether a trial should be stopped
The maximum number of total trials allowed before the sweep stops
The minimum improvement a trial must show between evaluations to continue

feedback: evaluation_interval sets the frequency at which the policy checks each trial. For example, evaluation_interval=1 means the policy is applied at every reporting interval. This is separate from delay_evaluation, which sets how many trials must complete before the policy starts checking at all.

question: What does delay_evaluation=5 mean in an early termination policy?

options.text: The policy waits 5 seconds before evaluating each trial
The policy will not terminate any trial until at least 5 trials have completed
The policy checks every 5th trial and skips the others
The sweep job is paused for 5 intervals before starting evaluations

feedback: delay_evaluation protects early trials from being terminated before there is enough data to make a meaningful comparison. With delay_evaluation=5, the policy doesn't apply at all until 5 trials have finished â€” regardless of evaluation_interval. This prevents premature termination when the best metric baseline isn't yet established.

question:
You configure a sweep job with these settings:

    BanditPolicy(slack_amount=0.2, delay_evaluation=5, evaluation_interval=1)
    max_total_trials=20

The best trial so far has accuracy=0.85. A new trial reports accuracy=0.60 at evaluation interval 8.

What happens to this trial?

options.text: It continues running â€” the delay_evaluation threshold has not been reached yet
It is terminated â€” 0.60 is more than 0.2 below the best metric of 0.85
It is terminated â€” it falls below the median of all trials
It continues running â€” max_total_trials has not been reached

feedback: With slack_amount=0.2 and best metric=0.85, any trial below 0.85 - 0.2 = 0.65 is terminated. Since 0.60 < 0.65, the trial is stopped. delay_evaluation=5 was already passed (we are at interval 8). max_total_trials is irrelevant to whether an individual poor-performing trial gets stopped early.

question: Which early termination policy should you use if you want to eliminate the bottom 20% of trials at each evaluation point â€” rather than comparing against the best single trial or the median?
feedback: TruncationSelectionPolicy is the only policy that works on a percentile basis â€” canceling the bottom X% of trials. BanditPolicy works by comparing against the best trial with a margin. MedianStoppingPolicy works by comparing against the running median. Truncation is the right choice when you want rank-based elimination.
